question: A policy analyst at a European banking supervisor is drafting the background section of a consultation on the December 2017 Basel III reforms. One paragraph must explain why the Basel Committee replaced the output floor that had been introduced under Basel II. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.A: The Basel II floor had been implemented inconsistently across countries, partly because it was based on Basel I standards that many banks and jurisdictions no longer applied.
options.B: The Basel II floor had restricted the capital benefit of internal models too severely, so the revised floor removes any limit on that benefit relative to standardised approaches.
options.C: The Basel II floor had applied only to banks using standardised approaches, so the revised floor extends a comparable minimum to banks using internal models.
options.D: The Basel II floor had been based on Basel III standardised approaches that proved miscalibrated, so the revised floor returns to Basel I capital requirements.

solution:
Stem summary: European supervisor’s consultation: why the Basel II output floor was replaced.

**Concept and theory**

An **output floor** stops a bank’s modelled capital from falling too far below a simpler benchmark. Under Basel II, GARP says, the floor was “based on Basel I capital requirements” and “calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I capital requirements.”

Why replace it? GARP gives two linked reasons: “Implementation of the Basel II floor has been inconsistent across countries, partly because of differing interpretations of the requirement and also because it is based on the Basel I standards, which many banks and jurisdictions no longer apply.” What replaced it: “The Basel III reforms replace the existing Basel II floor with a floor based on the revised Basel III standardised […]

question:
A treasury analyst at a Chinese joint-stock bank is preparing a note for the asset-liability committee on the implementation and impact of the December 2017 Basel III reforms. Her draft contains the following statements:

I. The revised standardised approach for credit risk and the revised IRB, CVA and operational risk frameworks are implemented from 1 January 2022.

II. A jurisdiction that implements only the standardised approaches, and none of the internal-model approaches, is compliant with the Basel framework.

III. Because the Basel framework sets maximum standards, a jurisdiction may not impose requirements that are more conservative than the reforms.

IV. The leverage ratio buffer for global systemically important banks is implemented from 1 January 2022.

Which of the statements are accurate?
solution:
Stem summary: Chinese bank ALCO note: four statements on implementation and impact of the 2017 reforms.

**Concept and theory**

The reforms were announced in December 2017 but took effect later, and they set a floor for national rules, not a ceiling. GARP’s Table 23.5 gives the implementation dates:

| Revision | Implementation date |
|---|---|
| Revised SA for credit risk; revised IRB; revised CVA; revised operational risk | 1 January 2022 |
| Revised market risk framework | 1 January 2022 |
| Leverage ratio: existing exposure definition | 1 January 2018 |
| Leverage ratio: revised exposure definition; G-SIB buffer | 1 January 2022 |
| Output floor | Phased in from 1 January 2022 |

question:
A senior credit risk analyst at a Canadian regional bank is presenting the December 2017 revisions to the standardized approach (SA) for credit risk to a group of newly hired analysts. Her draft slide contains the following statements:

I. The single risk weight previously applied to all residential mortgages is replaced by risk weights that depend on the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio of the mortgage.

II. Mechanical reliance on credit ratings is reduced by prohibiting the use of external credit ratings in every jurisdiction that adopts the revised SA.

III. Credit conversion factors for off-balance sheet items are made more risk sensitive, including positive conversion factors for unconditionally cancellable commitments.

IV. The risk-weight treatment of unrated exposures to banks is made less granular, with a single flat risk weight replacing the earlier treatment.

Which of the statements on the slide are accurate?
solution:
Stem summary: Canadian regional bank: audit of four slide statements on the revised standardized approach for credit risk.

**Concept and theory**

Credit risk accounts for the bulk of most banks’ risk taking and therefore of their regulatory capital. The standardized approach (SA) is the method most banks around the world use, including banks outside Basel Committee jurisdictions. Under the SA the bank does not model anything: it multiplies each exposure by a risk weight set by the regulator, and RWA is the sum. The weakness of the Basel II SA was that its risk weights were coarse. A single flat weight covered all residential mortgages, a flat weight covered unrated bank exposures, and the scheme leaned mechanically on external ratings.

An excerpt of the applicable risk weights and the loan data are shown below. Under the lender’s previous approach, every residential mortgage carried the same flat risk weight of 35%. Where the revised-SA criteria are not met, the applicable counterparty risk weight is 75%.

| Revised SA, general residential real estate (excerpt) | Risk weight |
|---|---|
| LTV below 50% | 20% |
| LTV 50% to 60% | 25% |
| Criteria not met (any LTV) | Risk weight of counterparty |

| Loan | Balance (AUD million) | LTV (%) | Revised-SA criteria met? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4.0 | 45 | Yes |
| 2 | 6.0 | 58 | Yes |
| 3 | 2.0 | 52 | No |

solution:
Stem summary: Australian mortgage lender: RWA of three residential mortgages under the revised SA whole loan approach.

**Concept and theory**

Under the Basel II SA, a mortgage at 45% LTV and a mortgage at 95% LTV attracted the same weight, even though the borrower with little equity is far riskier and the collateral cushion is far thinner. The December 2017 revision makes the risk weight a function of the LTV band, so RWA now tracks the collateral cushion. GARP Table 23.1 gives, for general residential real estate under the whole loan approach, 20% below 50% LTV and 25% for 50% to 60% LTV, with the weight rising across higher bands. Where the qualifying criteria are not met, the LTV table is not used at all: the risk weight of the counterparty applies to the whole exposure.

question:
The CRO of a German banking group with supervisory approval for both the foundation IRB (F-IRB) and advanced IRB (A-IRB) approaches is planning the transition to the revised IRB framework. The group has total assets of EUR 310 billion and currently uses an internal-model approach for each of the four portfolios below.

| Portfolio | Description |
|---|---|
| P1 | Loans to corporates with consolidated revenues of EUR 750 million |
| P2 | Listed and unlisted equity holdings |
| P3 | Project finance loans (specialized lending) |
| P4 | Interbank placements with other banks |

Which of the following correctly states the most advanced approach that remains available for each portfolio under the revised framework?

options.A: P1: F-IRB; P2: SA; P3: A-IRB; P4: F-IRB
options.B: P1: A-IRB; P2: SA; P3: A-IRB; P4: F-IRB
options.C: P1: F-IRB; P2: F-IRB; P3: A-IRB; P4: F-IRB
options.D: P1: F-IRB; P2: SA; P3: F-IRB; P4: F-IRB

solution:
Stem summary: German banking group: most advanced IRB approach still available for four portfolios.

**Concept and theory**

Under the IRB approaches the bank’s own models feed the Basel risk-weight function. In the advanced IRB (A-IRB) approach the bank estimates PD, LGD, EAD and maturity; in the foundation IRB (F-IRB) approach the bank estimates PD while LGD and EAD take fixed supervisory values. The crisis exposed three shortcomings: excessive complexity, lack of comparability of IRB capital across banks, and lack of robustness in modeling certain asset classes. The Committee therefore removed the A-IRB option for asset classes that cannot be modeled in a robust and prudent manner and removed IRB entirely for equities (GARP Table 23.2).

question:
A model validation analyst at a Japanese bank is checking parameter estimates for three IRB portfolios against the input floors in the revised IRB framework. Corporate X uses the A-IRB approach and Corporate Y uses the F-IRB approach, under which LGD is a supervisory value. All corporate exposures shown are unsecured.

| Portfolio | Approach | Bank PD (bp) | Bank LGD (%) | PD floor (bp) | LGD floor (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Corporate X | A-IRB | 3 | 20 | 5 | 25 |
| Corporate Y | F-IRB | 4 | n/a | 5 | 25 |
| Retail revolvers | A-IRB | 8 | 55 | 10 | 50 |

Which of the following sets of adjustments is required by the revised framework?

options.A: Raise X’s PD to 5 bp and its LGD to 25%, raise the revolvers’ PD to 10 bp, and leave Y’s PD at 4 bp, as floors bind only under A-IRB.
options.B: Raise X’s PD to 5 bp and its LGD to 25%, raise Y’s PD to 5 bp, and raise the revolvers’ PD to 10 bp.
options.C: Raise X’s PD to 5 bp and its LGD to 25%, raise Y’s PD to 5 bp, and lower the revolvers’ LGD to 50%.
options.D: Raise X’s PD and Y’s PD to 5 bp and the revolvers’ PD to 10 bp, and leave X’s LGD at 20%, as LGD floors apply only to secured exposures.

solution:
Stem summary: Japanese bank: applying revised IRB input floors to three portfolios.

**Concept and theory**

An input floor is a minimum value for a bank-estimated parameter. If the bank’s estimate is below the floor, the floor value is used; if the estimate is above the floor, the bank’s estimate stands. Floors exist to ensure a minimum level of conservatism in model parameters for asset classes where IRB remains available, and so to reduce unwarranted RWA variability across banks.

Which floors apply depends on which parameters the bank estimates:

| Floor | F-IRB | A-IRB |
|---|---|---|
| PD floor (bank estimates PD in both) | Applies | Applies |
| LGD floor | N/a (supervisory LGD) | Applies |
| EAD floor | Not applicable (supervisory EAD) | Applies if EAD modeled |

question: An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing a project memo that summarizes the December 2017 revisions to the IRB approaches for credit risk. Which of the following statements in the memo is most accurate?

options.A: Under F-IRB, banks estimate LGD and EAD while PD takes a fixed supervisory value, which removes two important sources of RWA variability.
options.B: The 1.06 scaling factor applied to IRB RWAs is retained, because the new input floors alone cannot remove unwarranted RWA variability.
options.C: For unsecured exposures to non-financial corporates, the supervisory F-IRB LGD is raised from 40% to 45% to add conservatism.
options.D: Under F-IRB, banks estimate PD while LGD and EAD take fixed supervisory values, which removes two important sources of RWA variability.

solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank audit: which memo statement on F-IRB and additional IRB enhancements is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The IRB revisions tackle RWA variability from three directions: (i) remove A-IRB where modeling is not robust; (ii) introduce input floors; (iii) specify estimation practices more tightly. Moving a portfolio from A-IRB to F-IRB matters because of who sets which parameter:

| Parameter | A-IRB | F-IRB |
|---|---|---|
| PD | Bank | Bank |
| LGD | Bank | Supervisor (fixed value) |
| EAD | Bank | Supervisor (fixed value) |

question: A risk consultant engaged by a Brazilian bank is presenting to its risk committee the three objectives behind the revised credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk framework. Which of the following pairs an objective with the design feature that the Basel Committee uses to achieve it?

options.A: Consistency: like the market risk approaches, the standardized approach rests on fair value sensitivities to market risk factors.
options.B: Risk sensitivity: the internally modeled approach is removed, because CVA risk cannot be modeled in a robust and prudent manner.
options.C: Robustness: the framework now captures the exposure component of CVA, which moves with transaction prices, along with its hedges.

solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank: pairing each CVA objective with the correct design feature.

**Concept and theory**

CVA risk is the risk of mark-to-market losses on derivatives caused by deterioration in a counterparty’s creditworthiness. GARP notes it was a major source of bank losses in the crisis, in some instances exceeding losses from outright defaults. The initial phase of Basel III introduced a CVA capital charge; the December 2017 revision reshaped it around three objectives:

| Objective | Design feature (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Enhance risk sensitivity | Capture the exposure component of CVA (which depends on the prices of the transactions and so on market risk factors) together with its associated hedges; the old framework omitted it. |

question:
The treasurer of a mid-sized Dutch bank is preparing for the revised CVA risk framework. Until now the bank has used an internally modeled approach for CVA risk. Its derivatives book is summarized below.

| Item | EUR billion |
|---|---|
| Aggregate notional, non-centrally cleared derivatives | 85.0 |
| Aggregate notional, centrally cleared derivatives | 140.0 |
| Counterparty credit risk capital charge | 0.9 |

Which of the following best describes how the bank may calculate its CVA capital charge under the revised framework?

options.A: It must use the standardized approach, because its total derivatives notional of EUR 225 billion exceeds the EUR 100 billion threshold.
options.B: It may keep its internally modeled approach, because its non-centrally cleared notional is below the EUR 100 billion threshold.
options.C: It may use the standardized or the basic approach, or set the charge as a simple multiplier of its counterparty credit risk charge.
options.D: It must set the charge as a simple multiplier of its counterparty credit risk charge, because this method is mandatory below EUR 100 billion.

solution:
Stem summary: Dutch bank: which CVA capital methods are available under the revised framework.

**Concept and theory**

After the revision, no bank may use an internal model for CVA risk. The framework consists of two approaches: the standardized approach (SA-CVA), based on fair value sensitivities, and the basic approach (BA-CVA), benchmarked to SA-CVA. GARP adds a proportionality option for smaller derivatives users: a bank with an aggregate notional amount of non-centrally cleared derivatives less than or equal to EUR 100 billion may calculate its CVA capital charge as a simple multiplier of its counterparty credit risk (CCR) charge.

question:

I. Operational risk capital requirements before the crisis proved insufficient to cover the operational risk losses incurred by some banks.

III. The new standardized approach assumes that operational risk increases with a bank’s income, but at a decreasing rate.

Before the reform, banks could use the advanced measurement approaches (AMA), based on internal models, or one of three standardized approaches. GARP identifies two shortcomings exposed by the crisis:

(i) Capital requirements for operational risk proved insufficient to cover the operational risk losses incurred by some banks.

(ii) The nature of the losses (events such as misconduct and inadequate systems and controls) highlighted how hard it is to estimate operational risk capital with internal models.

question: A policy analyst at a national banking regulator is briefing the regulator’s board on the internal loss multiplier (ILM) in the new standardized approach for operational risk, where capital equals the business indicator component (BIC) multiplied by the ILM. Which of the following statements in the briefing is most accurate?

options.A: The loss component equals 15 times the bank’s average annual operational risk losses over the preceding five years.
options.B: Where the supervisor sets the ILM equal to one, banks are no longer required to disclose their historical operational risk losses.
options.C: The ILM rises as the ratio of the loss component to the BIC rises, although it does so at a decreasing rate.
options.D: The ILM rises as the ratio of the loss component to the BIC rises, and it does so at an increasing rate.

solution:
Stem summary: Regulator board briefing: properties of the internal loss multiplier.

**Concept and theory**

The ILM converts a bank’s own loss history into a scaling of its income-based capital. Its inputs are:

- LC (loss component) = 15× the bank’s average historical operational risk losses over the preceding 10 years.
- BIC (business indicator component), the income-based measure.

ILM = ln$[e^{1} -$ 1 + $\left( \frac{\text{LC}}{\text{BIC}} \right)^{0.8}]$

When LC/BIC = 1, ILM = ln($e$) = 1. A bank whose losses are high relative to its BIC has LC$/\text{BIC} >$ 1 and ILM > 1; a bank with relatively low losses has ILM \< 1. question:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Risk-weighted G-SIB higher-loss absorbency requirement (%) | 1.5 |

| Tier 1 capital (JPY trillion) | 4.2 |

It currently reports a CET1 risk-weighted ratio of 6.80% and a Tier 1 leverage ratio of 3.20%. The applicable conservation standards are shown below.

| CET1 risk-weighted ratio | Tier 1 leverage ratio | Minimum capital conservation ratio (% of earnings) |
|---|---|---|
| 4.5% to 5.375% | 3% to 3.125% | 100% |
| above 5.375% to 6.25% | above 3.125% to 3.25% | 80% |
| above 6.25% to 7.125% | above 3.25% to 3.375% | 60% |

The leverage ratio buffer works like the risk-weighted buffers: it is divided into five ranges, and a G-SIB that falls into a range must retain a minimum percentage of earnings (capital distribution constraints). The constraints depend on two ratios:

- Tier 1 leverage ratio, against 3% minimum + G-SIB leverage buffer (here 0.5%): full requirement 3.5%.

question: The head of regulatory capital at a German universal bank with approval to use internal models is presenting the revised Basel III output floor to newly hired analysts. Which of the following statements best describes what the revised output floor does?

options.A: It places a minimum on Tier 1 capital relative to a non-risk-based exposure measure, acting as a backstop against excessive leverage at all banks.
options.B: It places a limit on the capital benefit that banks using internal models can derive relative to the standardised approaches, acting as a risk-based backstop.
options.C: It places a limit on the capital that banks using the standardised approaches must hold relative to internal models, acting as a ceiling on standardised RWAs.
options.D: It places a minimum on the bank-estimated PD, LGD and EAD values used as model inputs, acting as a floor on each modelled parameter.

solution:
Stem summary: German bank briefing: what the revised output floor does.

**Concept and theory**

Basel capital rules let a bank compute risk-weighted assets (RWAs) in two broad ways. The standardised approaches (SAs) apply regulator-set risk weights and formulas. Internal model approaches (for example IRB for credit risk) let a bank estimate risk parameters itself, subject to supervisory approval. Internal models usually produce lower RWAs than the SAs for the same exposures, and the financial crisis showed that such modelled requirements could be excessively complex, hard to compare across banks and not robust for some asset classes.

loText: Describe the revised output floor introduced as part of the Basel III reforms and approaches to be used when calculating the output floor.
question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Canadian bank is reviewing a briefing memo on the revised Basel III output floor. The memo contains the following statements:

I. The floor helps to maintain a level playing field between banks using internal models and banks on the standardised approaches.

II. The floor supports the credibility of banks’ risk-weighted calculations and improves comparability via the related disclosures.

III. Banks will be required to disclose their risk-weighted assets based on the revised standardised approaches.

IV. Once the floor is fully phased in, banks using internal models can no longer report total RWAs below their standardised-approach RWAs.

Which of the statements in the memo are accurate?
solution:
Stem summary: Canadian board risk committee: audit of four statements on the purpose and disclosure of the output floor.

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives three reasons for the revised floor beyond the basic “backstop” idea:

- **Level playing field.** Without a floor, two banks holding identical portfolios could report very different capital ratios simply because one uses internal models. The floor “helps to maintain a level playing field between banks using internal models and those on the standardised approaches.”
- **Credibility.** The crisis damaged confidence in modelled RWAs. The floor “supports the credibility of banks’ risk-weighted calculations”.
- **Comparability via disclosure.** It “improves comparability via the related disclosures”: banks “will also be required to disclose […]

question: A policy analyst at the UK prudential regulator is drafting a history note on the capital floor that the December 2017 Basel III reforms replaced with the revised output floor. Which of the following statements most accurately describes the floor that was replaced?

options.A: It was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I requirements, and was implemented inconsistently partly because many banks no longer apply Basel I standards.
options.B: It was calibrated at 72.5% of the relevant Basel I requirements, and was implemented inconsistently partly because many banks no longer apply Basel I standards.
options.C: It was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I requirements, and was implemented uniformly because all jurisdictions shared one interpretation of the rule.
options.D: It was calibrated at 80% of the revised Basel III standardised requirements, and was implemented inconsistently partly because of differing interpretations.

solution:
Stem summary: UK regulator history note: the floor replaced by the revised output floor.

**Concept and theory**

Floors are not new. GARP: “The Basel II framework introduced an output floor based on Basel I capital requirements. That floor was calibrated at 80% of the relevant Basel I capital requirements.” Its purpose was the same as today’s: stop banks moving to Basel II internal models from cutting capital too far below the older, simpler rules.

Why replace it? GARP: “Implementation of the Basel II floor has been inconsistent across countries, partly because of differing interpretations of the requirement and also because it is based on the Basel I standards, which many banks and jurisdictions no longer apply.” A floor measured against rules that banks no longer run is hard to compute […]

question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is estimating the bank’s total risk-weighted assets (RWAs) under the revised output floor, assuming the floor is fully phased in. The bank has supervisory approval for internal models for credit risk and market risk only. Her data are shown below; the approved column uses IRB for credit risk and internal models for market risk, while CVA risk (BA-CVA) and operational risk (standardised approach) are the same in both columns.

| Risk category | Approved approaches (JPY trillion) | Standardised approaches only (JPY trillion) |
|---|---|---|
| Credit risk | 30.0 | 46.0 |
| Market risk | 4.0 | 5.0 |
| CVA risk | 2.0 | 2.0 |
| Operational risk | 6.0 | 6.0 |
| Leverage ratio exposure measure |  | 150.0 |

Stem summary: Japanese bank: total RWAs after the fully phased-in output floor from a four-category table.

The revised floor compares two totals. GARP: “banks’ risk-weighted assets must be calculated as the higher of: (i) total risk-weighted assets calculated using the approaches that the bank has supervisory approval to use in accordance with the Basel capital framework (including both standardised and internal model-based approaches); and (ii) 72.5% of the total risk-weighted assets calculated using only the standardised approaches.”

question: The treasurer of a Singapore bank that uses internal models for most of its credit portfolio asks the bank’s risk consultant: “Once the revised output floor is fully phased in, how far can our approved approaches lower total RWAs relative to the standardised approaches before the floor starts to bind?” Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: By up to 27.5%: the floor binds when approved-approach RWAs fall below 72.5% of total standardised-only RWAs.
options.B: By up to 20%: the floor binds when approved-approach RWAs fall below 80% of total standardised-only RWAs.
options.C: By up to 72.5%: the floor binds when approved-approach RWAs fall below 27.5% of total standardised-only RWAs.
options.D: By up to 27.5%: the floor binds when total standardised-only RWAs fall below 72.5% of approved-approach RWAs.

solution:
Stem summary: Singapore bank: how far approved approaches can lower RWAs before the floor binds.

**Concept and theory**

The higher-of rule (Q4) can be read as a ratio test. Write

$r$ = $\frac{\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}}}{\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}} .$

The floor leg is 0.725 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$. The floor binds whenever $\text{RWA}_{\text{approved}} <$ 0.725 $\times\text{RWA}_{\text{SA only}}$, that is, whenever $r <$ 0.725. Equivalently, the maximum reduction internal models can deliver relative to the standardised approaches is 1 − 0.725 = 27.5%. This is the quantitative meaning of GARP’s phrase “limits the extent to which banks can lower their capital requirements relative to the standardised approaches.”

question:
An internal auditor at a French bank is reviewing the methodology the bank uses to compute the “standardised approaches only” leg of its output floor. The methodology document specifies the following treatments:

I. Derivatives counterparty credit risk: exposure measured with SA-CCR, then multiplied by the counterparty’s risk weight under the standardised approach for credit risk.

II. CVA risk: 100% of the bank’s counterparty credit risk capital requirement, this being the CVA treatment the bank is eligible for and uses.

III. Securitisation exposures: the internal ratings-based securitisation approach that the bank’s supervisor has approved for its main RWA calculation.

IV. Operational risk: the standardised approach for operational risk.

Which of the treatments are consistent with the Basel III requirements for calculating the output floor?
solution:
Stem summary: French bank internal audit: which methodology treatments fit the output floor rules.

**Concept and theory**

The floor’s second leg recomputes every risk type with a standardised (non-internal-model) method. GARP lists the approaches to be used:

| Risk type | Approach used for the floor |
|---|---|
| Credit risk | SA for credit risk; carrying value for credit risk mitigation (simple, or comprehensive with standard supervisory haircuts); includes failed trades and non-DvP transactions |

| CVA risk | SA-CVA, BA-CVA or 100% of CCR capital requirement, depending on which the bank is eligible for and uses |

question:
A junior risk analyst at a Swiss bank is building the output floor calculation for one netting set of over-the-counter interest rate derivatives with an unrated corporate counterparty. The bank has supervisory approval to model counterparty exposure internally and to use the IRB approach for this counterparty. The inputs are:

| Gross notional amount (EUR million) | 900.0 |

| Exposure under SA-CCR (EUR million) | 50.0 |

For derivatives, the floor leg needs two things, each standardised. question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank is computing total RWAs for reporting during calendar year 2026, using the output floor percentage that the Basel Committee’s transitional schedule sets from 1 January 2026. The supervisor has not exercised any discretion to cap the effect of the floor. The bank’s figures are:

| Item | BRL billion |
|---|---|
| Total RWAs under approved approaches (standardised and internal) | 500.0 |
| Total RWAs using only the standardised approaches | 900.0 |
| CET1 capital | 62.0 |

The bank’s total RWAs for 2026 after applying the output floor are closest to:

Stem summary: Brazilian bank: floored RWAs for 2026 under the transitional schedule.

The 72.5% calibration is the end point of a phase-in. GARP Table 23.5 (“Transitional Arrangement for Phasing in the Aggregate Output Floor”):

| From | Floor percentage (%) |
|---|---|
| 1 January 2022 | 50.0 |
| 1 January 2023 | 55.0 |
| 1 January 2024 | 60.0 |
| 1 January 2025 | 65.0 |
| 1 January 2026 | 70.0 |
| 1 January 2027 | 72.5 |

question:
The CRO of an Australian bank is reconstructing the bank’s total RWAs for 2025 for a back-testing review. The bank’s supervisor has exercised the national discretion available during the phase-in period to cap the increase in total RWAs that results from applying the output floor. The bank’s figures are:

| Item | AUD billion |
|---|---|
| Total RWAs under approved approaches, before the floor | 200.0 |
| Total RWAs using only the standardised approaches | 400.0 |

Using the output floor percentage applicable from 1 January 2025, the bank’s total RWAs for 2025 are closest to:
solution:
Stem summary: Australian bank: 2025 RWAs with the transitional cap exercised.

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “at national discretion, supervisors may cap the increase in a bank’s total RWAs that results from the application of the output floor during its phase-in period. The transitional cap on the increase in RWAs will be set at 25% of a bank’s RWAs before the application of the floor. question:
A supervisor at a national banking authority is preparing guidance on the transitional arrangements for the revised output floor. A draft lists the following statements:

I. Supervisors may, at national discretion, cap the increase in a bank’s total RWAs that results from applying the floor during its phase-in period.

II. Where the cap is used, it is set at 25% of the bank’s RWAs after the application of the floor.

III. The cap would be removed on 1 January 2027, when the floor reaches 72.5%.

IV. A jurisdiction may implement accelerated transitional arrangements, because the Basel framework constitutes minimum standards only.

Which of the statements are accurate?
solution:
Stem summary: National supervisor guidance: transitional arrangements for the output floor.

**Concept and theory**

The transitional arrangements around the floor have four features in GARP:

- **Discretion.** Supervisors may, at national discretion, cap the increase in total RWAs caused by the floor during its phase-in period. It is optional, not mandatory.

loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
question:
A researcher at a national regulatory agency is examining the use of the standardized ratings-based approach (SA) and the advanced internal ratings-based (A-IRB) approach in determining credit risk capital. The researcher evaluates the implications of applying these approaches to two different banks, Global Bank and Resource Bank. Information about the credit exposures of the two banks is provided below:

- Global Bank lends to large global corporations that have highly diverse business lines by providing sizable, long-dated unsecured credit facilities.
- Resource Bank lends to oil and gas producers in its region, most of which have small-scale operations. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion for the researcher to reach?

options.A: The A-IRB approach does not adjust for maturity, which means that A-IRB could undercapitalize the long-dated exposures at Global Bank.
options.B: The SA gives lower risk weights to unrated credits than to credits rated B+ or lower, which may incentivize Resource Bank to lend to unrated companies with poor credit quality.
options.C: Model parameters used in the SA effectively capture the high default correlation that is likely to exist between Resource Bank’s lending counterparties.
options.D: The A-IRB approach would require Global Bank to model the exposure at default while using a probability of default specified by the Basel committee.

solution:
**Concept**

Basel II credit risk. Standardized approach: risk weights from external ratings, with unrated corporates at 100% and those rated below B+ at 150%. Foundation IRB: the bank estimates PD. Advanced IRB: the bank estimates PD, LGD, EAD and maturity. Correlation is prescribed in both IRB approaches.

**Exam trap.** The unrated weight (100%) being lower than the weight for a poor rating (150%) gives weak borrowers a reason to stay unrated. The standardized approach has no correlation parameter at all.

loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
question: Pillar 1 of the Basel II framework allows banks to use various approaches to calculate the capital requirements for credit risk, operational risk, and market risk. Which of the following Basel II approaches allows a bank to use its own estimates of recovery rates?

options.A: The standardized measurement approach for operational risk
options.B: The advanced internal ratings-based approach for credit risk
options.C: The foundation internal ratings-based approach for credit risk
options.D: The fundamental review of the trading book (FRTB) approach for securitized products

solution:
**Concept**

Basel II credit risk. Standardized approach: risk weights from external ratings. Foundation IRB: the bank estimates PD only; LGD, EAD and maturity are set by the supervisor. Advanced IRB: the bank estimates PD, LGD, EAD and maturity. Recovery rate is 1 − LGD, so own recovery estimates mean own LGD.

**Exam trap.** Foundation versus advanced is a sibling pair that differs by which inputs the bank may estimate. PD in both; LGD and EAD only in advanced.

loText: Compare the standardized internal ratings-based (IRB) approach, the foundation IRB approach, and the advanced IRB approach for the calculation of credit risk capital under Basel II.
question: Under the IRB approach, banks are allowed to use their internal rating systems conditional on approval by their supervisors. If a bank was to use the foundation IRB approach, then it would have to use:

options.B: A predetermined estimate of PD based on the size of the bank
options.C: Its internal estimates of exposure-at-default (EAD) and the loss-given-default (LGD)
options.D: Predetermined estimates of EAD and LGD based on the size of the bank

solution:
**Concept**

Under both internal ratings-based approaches the bank’s capital comes from a supervisory formula. Foundation IRB: the bank supplies its own PD; LGD, EAD and maturity are prescribed. Advanced IRB: the bank supplies PD, LGD, EAD and maturity.

**Exam trap.** Option D is nearly right, which is what makes it dangerous: the values are predetermined, but “based on the size of the bank” is false.

loText: Calculate credit risk capital under Basel II utilizing the IRB approach.
question:
A regulatory analyst at a large bank is preparing a report of the bank’s credit risk capital for the current year and uses the Basel II IRB approach for making the calculation. As part of this process, the analyst identifies a portfolio of credit exposures of equal size that are held by borrowers with the same probability of default. The analyst has collected the following information about the portfolio:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Exposure at default | EUR 200 million |
| 1-year expected loss on the portfolio | EUR 4.2 million |
| Expected recovery rate on a defaulted credit | 30.00% |
| 1-year portfolio default rate at the 95th percentile | 5.66% |
| 1-year portfolio default rate at the 99.9th percentile | 9.87% |

What is the correct estimate of the Basel II credit risk capital that the bank should reserve for this portfolio?
solution:
**Concept**

Basel II IRB capital is unexpected loss at the 99.9th percentile: Capital $= \text{EAD}\times\text{LGD}\times\text{WCDR}_{99.9\%} -$EL, where the worst-case default rate comes from the Vasicek model and LGD = 1 − recovery rate.

**Working**

Capital $= 200 \times(1 - 0.30) \times0.0987 - 4.2 = 13.82 - 4.2 = \text{EUR} 9.62$ million

**Exam trap.** Three ways to go wrong, each an option: use the 95th percentile, use the recovery rate in place of LGD, or forget to subtract expected loss.

loText: Summarize the December 2017 revisions to the Basel III framework in the following areas: - The standardized approach to credit risk - The internal ratings-based (IRB) approaches for credit risk - The CVA risk framework - The operational risk framework - The leverage ratio framework
question: The CRO of a large bank has asked a group of risk managers to prepare a plan to implement the revisions to the Basel III guidelines finalized in December 2017. The bank expects to qualify as a global systemically important bank (G-SIB) by the time the revisions are implemented. Which of the following actions is most appropriate for the bank to take to comply with the revised Basel lll guidelines?

options.A: Introduce an internally created model to determine the bank’s operational risk capital.
options.B: Assign different credit risk weights for residential mortgages based on each mortgage’s loan-to-value ratio.
options.C: Apply the advanced internal rating-based approach for certain types of credit exposures, such as exposures to banks and large corporations.
options.D: Decrease the bank’s target level of its countercyclical buffer and its Basel III Tier 1 leverage ratio.

solution:
**Concept**

December 2017 Basel III reforms. Credit risk standardized approach: more granular risk weights, for example residential mortgages weighted by loan-to-value ratio. IRB: advanced IRB removed for banks, other financial institutions and large corporates. Operational risk: one standardised approach replaces internal models. Leverage ratio: a buffer for G-SIBs. Output floor: 72.5% of standardised RWA.

**Exam trap.** Every wrong option runs against the direction of the reforms, which reduce the role of internal models and tighten requirements.
